newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore fines opposition leaders for contempt.
newsitem.headline: Singapore fines opposition leaders for contempt.

text.p: Singapore's parliament on Wednesday accepted a recommendation by a committee to fine four opposition leaders a total of S$51,000 (US$36,455) for contempt of parliament involving misleading health spending figures.
A legislator from the opposition Workers' Party was the only MP to abstain from voting on a motion to accept the recommendation.

Singapore Democratic Party (SDP) Secretary General Chee Soon Juan was fined S$25,000 while three other SDP members were fined between S$5,000 and S$13,000. The maximum punishment for contempt of parliament is a S$50,000 fine and a jail term.
Chee and the others could have been barred from contesting the general election due by April 1997 if the case had been passed to a civil court which then found against them.
But since parliament decided to heed the parliamentary committee's recommendations, it should leave the four free to contest the poll.

Chee told Reuters he would withhold comment until he had a chance to study the parliament's decision, particularly whether the party could pay the fine and whether he would be allowed to run in the elections.
In a statement following the committee's report on November 22, Chee said fines would deal the party a serious financial setback but that it would continue to speak up for Singaporeans.
The committee found that Chee had fabricated data and falsified documents submitted to a select committee on health and misled the committee when it challenged the figures.
An SDP document submitted to the health committee in August claimed that the government's share of total health expenditure had dropped to five percent in 1990 from 40 percent in 1970.
The 1990 figure was incorrect and should have been 25.4 percent, the SDP later admitted. Chee told the committee of privileges the figure was a typing mistake and a result of human error.

Leader of the House Wong Kan Seng, who introduced the motion to fine Chee and the others, said some might argue that the ruling party used the committee of privileges as a political weapon against its opponents.
But Wong said: "It is a person's conduct, not his or her party affiliation, which determines whether he or she appears before the committee of privileges."

The motion to fine the four SDP leaders, who are not elected MPs, was first tabled on December 2 but was postponed because the party's three MPs were absent. Two of three SDP legislators were again absent from Wednesday's sitting.
